title: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions

guide.summary: Unit 4 builds the probability tools behind inference: simulation, basic probability rules, conditional probability and independence, discrete random variables (mean and standard deviation), combining and transforming random variables, and the binomial and geometric distributions.

sections.heading: Probability rules
sections.body: Probability is the long-run relative frequency of an outcome. Simulation estimates probabilities by modeling a chance process many times; a complete description states how random digits or numbers represent outcomes, how many are taken per trial, whether repeats are allowed, and what is recorded. Complement rule: P(Aᶜ) = 1 − P(A). Addition rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B); for mutually exclusive events, P(A and B) = 0. Conditional probability: P(A | B) = P(A and B)/P(B). Events are independent if P(A | B) = P(A); then P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B). Mutually exclusive events with nonzero probabilities can never be independent. Tree diagrams organize multistage problems, including 'reverse' conditional probabilities such as P(disease | positive test).

sections.heading: Discrete random variables
sections.body: A probability distribution lists the values of X and their probabilities, which sum to 1. Mean (expected value): μ_X = Σx·P(x), the long-run average. Standard deviation: σ_X = √Σ(x − μ)²P(x). Interpret the mean as a long-run average over many repetitions, not a value expected on a single trial.

sections.heading: Transforming and combining
sections.body: For Y = a + bX: μ_Y = a + bμ_X and σ_Y = |b|σ_X. For sums and differences: μ_{X±Y} = μ_X ± μ_Y always. If X and Y are independent, variances add: σ²_{X±Y} = σ²_X + σ²_Y (even for differences). For the total of n independent observations of X, σ = √n·σ_X, which differs from multiplying one observation by n (σ = n·σ_X). If X and Y are Normal and independent, X ± Y is Normal.

sections.heading: Binomial and geometric distributions
sections.body: Binomial setting (BINS): Binary outcomes, Independent trials, fixed Number of trials n, Same probability p. P(X = k) = C(n,k)pᵏ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ; μ = np, σ = √(np(1 − p)). Use binompdf for exactly k and binomcdf for at most k; 'at least one' = 1 − P(none). When sampling without replacement, treat trials as independent if n ≤ 10% of the population. Geometric setting counts trials until the first success: P(X = k) = (1 − p)ᵏ⁻¹p, μ = 1/p, σ = √(1 − p)/p.

sections.heading: Worked example: binomial probability
sections.body: A basketball player makes 70% of free throws. If she shoots 10, the number made X follows a binomial distribution with n = 10 and p = 0.7, assuming independent shots. P(X = 8) = C(10, 8)(0.7)⁸(0.3)² ≈ 0.233. The mean is np = 7 made shots and the standard deviation is √(np(1 − p)) = √2.1 ≈ 1.45. P(X ≥ 9) = P(9) + P(10) ≈ 0.121 + 0.028 = 0.149.

sections.heading: Worked example: combining random variables
sections.body: If X has mean 50 and standard deviation 6 and Y has mean 30 and standard deviation 8, and X and Y are independent, then X + Y has mean 80 and standard deviation √(36 + 64) = 10. X − Y has mean 20 and also standard deviation 10, because variances add for both sums and differences of independent variables. Multiplying a variable by a constant multiplies its mean and standard deviation by that constant.

sections.heading: Probability rules in practice
sections.body: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). Events are mutually exclusive if they cannot occur together, and independent if P(A | B) = P(A). Conditional probability P(A | B) = P(A and B)/P(B). Tree diagrams and two-way tables organize multistep probability problems.

sections.heading: Common errors
sections.body: Students add standard deviations instead of variances, confuse independent and mutually exclusive events, and use binomial models when trials are not independent or the number of trials is not fixed.

sections.heading: Key terms
sections.body: Know sample space, event, complement, independence, conditional probability, random variable, expected value, binomial and geometric distributions.

sections.heading: Free-response connection
sections.body: Probability questions often combine several ideas: a conditional probability from a tree diagram, then a binomial calculation based on that probability. Define the random variable, state the distribution and its parameters, and show the calculation, including the formula or calculator command with labeled inputs.

keyTakeaways: Means always add; variances add only for independent variables.
Y = a + bX: mean a + bμ, SD |b|σ.
Binomial: fixed n; geometric: trials until first success.
commonMistakes: Adding standard deviations instead of variances.
Using binomial when the number of trials isn't fixed.
Confusing P(A | B) with P(B | A).
examTips: Define random variables in words and name the distribution with parameters (e.g., 'X ~ Binomial, n = 10, p = 0.3').
Show the formula or label calculator inputs for every probability.
Tree diagrams earn credit on conditional-probability FRQs.
For combining random variables, state that independence is needed for the SD.
guide.cramSheet:

vocab.definition: The set of all possible outcomes of a chance process.
Events that cannot occur at the same time.
Events for which knowing one occurred does not change the probability of the other.
The probability of one event given that another has occurred.
A variable whose numerical value is determined by a chance process.
The long-run average value of a random variable over many repetitions.
A list or rule giving the possible values of a random variable and their probabilities.
The distribution of the number of successes in n independent trials with the same success probability.
The distribution of the number of trials needed to get the first success.
When sampling without replacement, trials can be treated as independent if the sample is at most 10% of the population.
Imitating a chance process to estimate probabilities.
As the number of trials increases, the relative frequency approaches the true probability.

practice.stem: What is the expected value of X?
A basketball player makes 20% of her half-court shots, independently. What is the probability her first make occurs on her third attempt?
Events A and B are mutually exclusive, with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.5. Which is true?

choices.text: A and B are independent.
P(A and B) = 0.15.
A and B are not independent, because P(A | B) = 0 ≠ P(A).

practice.explanation: If B occurs, A cannot, so knowing B changes A's probability to 0.

distractors.B: Would be true only if independent.

choices.text: Mean 4, SD 1
Mean 4, SD 7
Mean 16, SD 5
Mean 4, SD 5

practice.stem: For a randomly chosen resident, are owning a pet and living in a house independent?

choices.text: No, because P(pet | house) = 0.60 is not equal to P(pet) = 0.48
Yes, because both events have probabilities between 0 and 1
Yes, because P(pet and house) = 0.36
No, because the events are mutually exclusive

practice.topic: 4.8 Mean and Standard Deviation of Random Variables
practice.stem: The number of defects X on a circuit board has mean 1.7 and SD 0.9. Each defect costs $3 to repair, plus a fixed $2 inspection fee. What are the mean and SD of the total cost?

distractors.B: Adds the fixed fee to the SD.

To simulate whether a 70% free-throw shooter makes a shot, a student uses random digits 0–9. Which assignment is correct?

choices.text: Digits 0–6 represent a make; 7–9 represent a miss.
Digits 0–7 represent a make; 8–9 represent a miss.
Digit 7 represents a make; all others a miss.

practice.explanation: Seven of ten equally likely digits (0–6) gives probability 0.7.

practice.stem: A disease affects 1% of a population. A test is positive for 95% of people with the disease and for 5% of people without it. If a randomly selected person tests positive, what is the probability they have the disease?
Bags of flour have weights that are Normal with mean 500 g and SD 10 g, independently. A box holds 4 bags. What is the probability that a box's total flour weight is less than 1,970 g?

distractors.A: Uses the SD of one bag (10 g): z = −3.

practice.stem: Which situation is best modeled by a binomial distribution?

choices.text: The number of left-handed people in a random sample of 50 from a city of 300,000, where 10% are left-handed
The number of hearts in 5 cards dealt from a standard 52-card deck without replacement
The number of cards drawn from a standard deck until an ace appears
The total weight of 10 randomly chosen apples

practice.explanation: Fixed n = 50, success/failure, p ≈ 0.10, and 50 is far less than 10% of the city, so trials are approximately independent.

distractors.B: 5 cards is about 10% of a 52-card deck, and drawing without replacement noticeably changes p from card to card.
distractors.C: No fixed number of trials (geometric-type setting).

practice.topic: 4.8 Mean and Standard Deviation of Random Variables
practice.stem: A raffle ticket costs $5. One ticket in 1,000 wins $2,000, and 10 tickets in 1,000 win $100. Which statement about the buyer's net gain is correct?

choices.text: Each buyer will lose exactly $2.00.
The expected net gain is $3.00.
The expected net gain is −$5.00, because most tickets lose.
The expected net gain is −$2.00, so over many tickets a buyer loses about $2 per ticket on average.

practice.explanation: Expected winnings = 2,000(0.001) + 100(0.010) = $3.00; net = 3 − 5 = −$2.00, a long-run average.

distractors.A: Expected value describes the long-run average, not each outcome.

practice.topic: 4.8 Mean and Standard Deviation of Random Variables
practice.prompt: At a school fair, a game costs $2 to play. The player rolls a fair six-sided die. A 6 wins $5, a 4 or 5 wins $1, and 1, 2, or 3 wins nothing. Let X = the player's net gain (winnings minus the $2 cost).

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Construct the probability distribution of X.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate and interpret the expected value of X.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A player plays 3 games. Calculate the probability of rolling at least one 6.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Let G = the number of games until the player first rolls a 6. Identify the distribution of G and calculate P(G ≤ 4).

rubric.description: E(X) = 3(1/6) − 1(2/6) − 2(3/6) = −5/6 ≈ −$0.83; over many games, a player loses about $0.83 per game on average.

practice.sampleResponse:
(a)

| X (net gain, $) | 3 | −1 | −2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| P(X) | 1/6 | 2/6 | 3/6 |

(b) E(X) = 3(1/6) + (−1)(2/6) + (−2)(3/6) = (3 − 2 − 6)/6 = −5/6 ≈ −$0.83. If a player plays this game many, many times, the player's net gain will average about −$0.83 per game; that is, they will lose about 83 cents per game in the long run.

(c) Rolls are independent with P(6) = 1/6. P(at least one 6) = 1 − P(no 6 in 3 games) = 1 − (5/6)³ ≈ 0.421.

(d) G follows a geometric distribution with p = 1/6. P(G ≤ 4) = 1 − P(no 6 in the first 4 games) = 1 − (5/6)⁴ ≈ 0.518.
